nasa-tm-19640023710-long-period-contribu:
T. L. Felsentreger and W. J. Wickless of Goddard wrote this paper in August 1964. It treats slow drifts in satellite orbits caused by Earth's uneven gravity. Those uneven pulls are summed up as zonal harmonics in the title. The seventh, ninth, and eleventh harmonics are its focus.

Catalog notes say the paper gives formulas for long-period terms. Such terms build up slowly over many orbits of a satellite. Ignoring them makes predicted positions wander off over time. Higher harmonics refine the gravity map beyond the main bulge terms. The work is pure orbit bookkeeping, the kind of math that kept early satellite tracking honest.
nasa-tm-19670006712-ground-test-faciliti:
John R. Esterly, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, gave this lecture at the University of Tennessee Space Institute in Tullahoma on January 31, 1967. It formed one of thirty-two lectures in a two-week course on aerospace test facilities. Esterly's subject is the ground facilities needed to develop and evaluate advanced airbreathing engines, the jet engines that power aircraft.

Esterly traces how flight progress has always followed engine progress, from early gasoline engines to the Wright brothers and Glenn Curtiss. As engines and aircraft grew more complex, he argues, ground test facilities took on a central support role. Good facilities let engineers solve altitude and high-speed problems on the ground. That avoids flight tests that would otherwise be costly, hazardous, and slow.
nasa-tm-19680001473-decontamination-tech:
Francis N. LeDoux, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, explains how to clean a spacecraft bound for the Moon, in October 1966. The worry is biological: Earth microbes riding along could confuse the search for lunar life. Every lunar orbiter or lander had to be made biologically clean.

NASA's quarantine office ruled that full sterilization was not required for the Moon. The Moon's harsh surface would keep any contamination local, the office reasoned. Still, viable organisms had to be cut to a low level before launch. LeDoux developed decontamination methods for the AIMP spacecraft series. A test program first checked that parts could survive the cleaning chemicals.
